cards.explanation: The answer is True, friends. The writer says it's pleasing when you keep the words “…within you and they are constantly on your lips.” So they live inside you AND they come out of your mouth. Wisdom that never leaves the building is like a batch of cookies nobody's allowed to touch.

The goal is trust in the LORD, friends. The writer says, “So that your trust may be in the LORD, I instruct you today…” Every saying in this section points back to that one target. Not a trophy, not a crowd, just trust in the LORD.

The answer is those who sent you, friends. The writer says these true and reliable words are given “…that you may soundly answer those who sent you?” That's how the verse puts it. The text doesn't say who sent you, so I'll leave that open, too.

The answer is the LORD, friends. The writer says, “…for the LORD will take up their case and will plunder those who rob them.” The poor man doesn't have to carry that case alone. Somebody bigger than any bully is on it.

The reason is that you may learn his ways and get caught in a snare, friends. The writer says, “…or you may learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.” Notice the word "may." The danger he names is picking up the angry man's ways. I've picked up a few habits from my years in a junk drawer myself, and I'm still shaking some of them.

Your own bed is what could be taken, friends. The writer asks, “If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?” That's a pretty rough picture. Imagine the debt collector showing up and the thing he wants is where you sleep.

The answer is False, friends. The writer says, “Do not move an ancient boundary stone which your fathers have placed.” He doesn't add any exceptions for needing a little extra yard. The stone stays right where your fathers set it.

The answer is kings, friends. The writer says the man skilled in his work “…will be stationed in the presence of kings; he will not stand before obscure men.” Good work gets noticed. I'd like to say my smudged cookies prove the same thing, but they mostly prove I have mustache problems.

The answer is that the food is deceptive, friends. The writer says, “Do not crave his delicacies, for that food is deceptive.” He doesn't spell out how it deceives, and I won't make that up for him. The warning is plain: delicacies on a ruler's table, and the writer still says don't crave them.

The answer is False, friends. The writer says, “Do not wear yourself out to get rich; be wise enough to restrain yourself.” He doesn't say work is bad, but he says don't wear yourself out chasing riches. Restraint is the wise move here, and the writer says so.

The point is that riches don't stay with you, friends. The writer says, “When you glance at wealth, it disappears, for it makes wings for itself and flies like an eagle to the sky.” You look, and it's already leaving. It's like trying to hold on to a warm cookie in a room full of hungry people.

He's inwardly counting the cost, friends. The writer says the stingy man “…is keeping track, inwardly counting the cost.” He says, “Eat and drink…” but the writer adds, “…his heart is not with you.” The words say one thing and the inside says another.

The answer is True, friends. The writer says, “You will vomit up what little you have eaten and waste your pleasant words.” So the meal doesn't stay down, and the pleasant words are wasted too. It's a rough ending for a dinner invitation.

The word is despise, friends. The writer says, “Do not speak to a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words.” Some folks hear good words and just roll their eyes. The writer says to save your breath.

The answer is the fatherless, friends. The writer says, “Do not move an ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless…” The stone warning comes back with a new group added to it. So the stone and the fields both stay as they are.

The writer says their Redeemer is strong, friends. He says, “…for their Redeemer is strong; He will take up their case against you.” The fatherless have a Redeemer who takes up their case. That's worth knowing before anybody moves a boundary stone.

The answer is False, friends. The writer says, “Do not withhold discipline from a child…” So he's saying not to hold it back. It's one of the heavier sayings in the passage, so I'll leave it at what the verse says.
